newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: LG-Caltex the biggest Asian buyer of Alaskan crude.
newsitem.headline: LG-Caltex the biggest Asian buyer of Alaskan crude.

text.p: LG-Caltex Oil Corp, South Korea's joint-venture company with oil major Caltex, emerged on Friday as Asia's largest long-term buyer of Alaskan North Slope crude oil.

LG-Caltex has agreed to import 30,000 barrels per day (bpd) of Alaskan North Slope (ANS) crude from British Petroleum Co Plc (BP). The agreement becomes effective on December 20, a company statement said on Friday.

LG-Caltex, a joint venture between LG Group and Caltex Petroleum Corp, itself a joint venture between U.S. oil giants Texaco Inc and Chevron Corp, said the purchase agreement would be extended annually unless either side raised objections.
"We will be importing 800,000 to 1.3 million barrels of ANS a month which should total about 10.6 million barrels a year," said a head trader of LG-Caltex.
The refiner declined to disclose the exact price structure of the deal, but said the Alaskan crude imports were expected to raise LG-Caltex's annual crude oil import costs by $240 million.
The refiner said BP had agreed to take responsibility for delivery and compensate for possible accidents in loading and unloading the cargoes.
"The deal was very favourable for us," said the head trader, pointing to savings in delivery costs.

Alaska is geographically closer to South Korea than Middle East countries. The refiner said it would take an average of 12 days to ship crude to South Korea from Alaska, compared with 22-27 days from the Middle East.

Traders said Alaskan crude, which is low in sulphur and similar to Omani crude, is desirable given South Korea's current lack of cracking facilities -- a refinery process to produce distillates -- and strong demand for low-sulphur crudes.

The deal also helps to reduce LG-Caltex's reliance on Middle East crude to 50 percent of imports and join in the South Korean government's efforts to diversify its crude supply sources, the company said. Middle East nations provide more than 70 percent of South Korea's crude demand at present.

LG-Caltex said the commitment also comes before its new 220,000-bpd crude distillation unit goes commercial later this month. The unit will double LG-Caltex's licensed crude processing capacity to 600,000 bpd from the current 380,000 bpd.

"With our refinery capacity expanding we were looking for a profitable deal that would also provide supply stability," the LG-Caltex trader said. "We expect the ANS deal to put downward pressure on the price of the Middle East crude."
Other oil companies are also interested in buying the Alaskan crude.
"We are holding talks with BP on a long-term deal," said a crude trader at Yukong Ltd, which last month expanded refining capacity by 200,000 bpd to 810,000 bpd.
South Korea currently has a total refining capability of 2.22 million bpd.
"I know Hyundai Oil and Japanese and Chinese oil refiners are also in talks with BP for possible long-term contracts," the Yukong trader said.
Traders said BP has been actively seeking long-term ANS buyers. BP became a large equity holder in the Alaskan oil fields after the lifting of a ban on ANS crude exports in May.
In February Taiwan's state-owned Chinese Petroleum Corp signed a one-year agreement with BP for the supply of 10,000 to 15,000 bpd of ANS.
